title: The name on the meat
hook: the animal is killed swiftly, with Allah's name, a sharp blade, and mercy

segments.voice: Yesterday: tayyib, good and wholesome, not just permitted. Your line was lawful and good. Did you ask both questions at a meal? Day one hundred forty-five.

Most of us eat meat without ever thinking about the moment the animal died. It arrives on a foam tray under plastic, and the story before that is somebody else's business. Islam doesn't let that moment disappear. Halal meat isn't just about which animals. It's about how. There's a name that has to be said. There's a blade that has to be sharp. And there's a hadith that puts one word over the whole thing, a word you wouldn't expect at a slaughterhouse. Today: the name on the meat.
screen: `A FOAM TRAY UNDER PLASTIC.` → `NOT JUST WHICH ANIMAL, BUT HOW.` → `A WORD YOU WOULDN'T EXPECT.`

segments.voice: The word is dhabihah, an animal slaughtered in the prescribed way. The core of it is simple. The one slaughtering says the name of Allah, usually bismillah, Allahu akbar. Then one swift cut across the throat with a very sharp blade, so it is over quickly and the blood drains out, since the Qur'an forbids eating blood. The name comes from the Qur'an: in Surah al-An'am, believers are told to eat of what Allah's name has been said over, and not of what it hasn't. The name is a reminder that this life wasn't yours to begin with. You're taking it with permission, not by right. Then the word. Sahih Muslim reports, from Shaddad ibn Aws, that the Prophet ﷺ said: Allah has written ihsan on everything. Ihsan means excellence, beauty, doing a thing as well as it can be done. So when you slaughter, slaughter well. Let each of you sharpen his blade, and spare the animal suffering. Other reports go further: don't sharpen the knife where the animal can see, and don't slaughter one animal in front of another. The same collections tell of a man forgiven for giving water to a thirsty dog, and a woman punished for starving a cat. Mercy even here, at the hardest moment. Muslims differ on some modern questions. Scholars disagree about stunning before slaughter, and about whether ordinary meat from Jews and Christians, whose food the Qur'an calls lawful, still counts today. But the principle underneath isn't disputed: say the name, keep the blade sharp, and be kind.
screen: `DHABIHAH — THE NAME AND THE CUT.` · `EAT WHAT HIS NAME WAS SAID OVER.` · `IHSAN IS WRITTEN ON EVERYTHING.` · `SCHOLARS DIFFER ON MODERN QUESTIONS.` · then, large: `MERCY EVEN HERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say bismillah before eating. Bukhari reports that the Prophet told a young boy at his table: say the name of Allah, eat with your right hand, and eat from what's in front of you. So picture your next meal. Before the first bite, pause. If you pray, you can say bismillah, in the name of Allah. If not, simply pause, and remember that something gave itself for this plate, a plant or an animal, and someone grew it, caught it or cooked it. One breath of thanks. Then sit with that. The bell holds the time.
Dhabihah. Meat slaughtered in the prescribed way: Allah's name, a swift cut with a sharp blade, and mercy. Today's word.
Your line: mercy even here. At every meal today, pause before the first bite, say the name or a word of thanks, and remember what it cost. Day one hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Halal meat comes from an animal slaughtered with Allah's name spoken, one swift cut with a sharp blade, the blood drained, and care to spare it suffering; Muslims also say bismillah before eating.

fork.setup: you're about to slaughter a sheep for a family meal. the knife is a little dull. what does the hadith say?
options: dull is fine, just work harder
sharpen your blade and spare the animal suffering
fork.reveal: let each of you sharpen his blade and spare his animal suffering (Muslim 1955). mercy even at the hardest moment.

original.note: Arabic: an animal slaughtered in the prescribed way, from dhabaha, to slaughter.

trapdoor: what you thought: halal meat is just meat a Muslim blessed.
what it means: it's a way of slaughter with the name, a swift cut, the blood drained, and mercy.
what a scholar hears: 6:118–121 on the name; 5:3 on blood; ihsan in Muslim 1955; 5:5 and the modern debates on stunning and Ahl al-Kitab.
